signal_stats.confounding_explanation: Metformin is pharmacologically classified as an antihyperglycemic agent rather than a hypoglycemic agent. It works primarily by inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis and increasing peripheral insulin sensitivity without stimulating insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells. Consequently, metformin monotherapy carries a negligible risk of hypoglycemia. The high PRR observed in FAERS is almost entirely driven by the common clinical practice of prescribing metformin in combination with insulin secretagogues (sulfonylureas, meglitinides) or exogenous insulin, which are the primary drivers of hypoglycemia in patients with type 2 diabetes. The signal is a classic example of confounding by co-medication.

mechanism.plausibility_rationale: While the mechanism involves inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis, AMPK activators like metformin do not typically cause hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy because they do not stimulate insulin secretion and the body retains compensatory mechanisms to maintain glucose levels. Hypoglycemia is generally only a risk when these agents are combined with insulin or insulin secretagogues.
